reviewBoundary: Three complete junior paired insertion practices: grade7 two5-of6 passages, grade8 two4-of5 diaries, grade9 two5-of7 guides with three printed headings, quoted gap2 and heading gap5.28 scoring slots. Same-author cohesion/all-candidate review only, no independent calibration.

units.title: Two stories: a puppet and a gate sign
units.alignmentNote: Two complete five-gap/six-candidate passages, one unused in each. New narratives; source supplies response form only.

materials.title: The puppet with a long nose
materials.instruction: Read the whole passage. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Our class made puppets for a short play. Mine was an old man with a hat and a very long paper nose. I thought the nose was the funniest part. ____1____ The audience would see it before they heard his first line.

At rehearsal, the nose caught on the edge of the little stage. I tried to lift the puppet higher. ____2____ He seemed to be looking at the ceiling instead of at the other character.

Our teacher asked me to try a shorter nose. I was disappointed, but I made one from spare paper. ____3____ This time, I could turn the puppet without catching it on anything.

My friend said the old man's voice was funny too. I practised saying the line slowly, then very quickly. ____4____ The slower version gave everyone time to understand why he was confused.

At the show, people laughed at the right moment. They did not know about the first nose. I kept both versions in my art folder afterwards. ____5____ The final puppet had become more enjoyable because I could use it well.
candidates: A. That solved one problem but made another.
B. We repeated the scene with the new shape.
C. I imagined it making everyone laugh.
D. They reminded me how the design had changed.
E. The puppet never appeared in any rehearsal or show.
F. We compared the two ways of speaking.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C introduces expected audience laughter, developed by first visual impression. A problem/B retry/F voice/D stored versions belong later; E contradicts events.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A links lifting solution with wrong gaze described next. Other candidates do not introduce the new posture problem.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: B follows shorter-nose making and prepares successful turn this time. Others do not describe re-running the scene.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: F names comparison of fast/slow speech, with next sentence favouring slower. Other choices concern shape or storage.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: D refers to both versions kept and leads to design/use conclusion. E denies rehearsal/show and other options describe earlier steps.

materials.title: A sign by the small gate
materials.instruction: Read the whole passage. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Our school garden has two gates. Visitors usually find the large one first, but it is kept closed during gardening lessons. We enter through the smaller gate beside the shed. ____1____ A new visitor could easily wait at the wrong place.

I offered to make a sign. My first message said only "Come this way". I put it beside the large gate and showed it to a friend. ____2____ From where she stood, the words gave no direction at all.

We added an arrow and the words "Small gate beside the shed". The teacher checked the route before we put it up. ____3____ A sign should not send people along a path that is blocked.

On Friday, I watched a visitor stop at the large gate, read the sign and walk towards the shed. ____4____ I still asked whether she needed help, but she said she had found the way.

The sign was taken down after the lesson because the entry arrangement could change on other days. ____5____ We kept it in the garden cupboard for the next time the same route was used.
candidates: A. This time, the arrow led her to the correct entrance.
B. She asked which way I meant.
C. Both gates were always open throughout every lesson.
D. We checked that the space beside the shed was clear.
E. That difference was obvious to us, but not to everyone.
F. We did not want a temporary instruction to look permanent.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: E contrasts familiar pupils with new visitors, developed by wrong-place risk. B unclear message/D path check/A successful visitor/F temporary sign fit later; C contradicts gate closure.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: B supplies friend’s direction question, explained by words lacking arrow. Others do not describe her response to first sign.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: D describes actual path check and prepares blocked-route caution. Other options address wording/use/duration.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A completes observed visitor following arrow, before she confirms no help needed. Other candidates describe other times.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: F explains removal after lesson and possible changed entry. Others do not distinguish temporary instruction from permanence.

units.title: Two diaries: a flower and a receipt
units.alignmentNote: Two complete four-gap/five-candidate diaries; each candidate at most once and one unused in each.

materials.title: Drawing the flower twice
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Wednesday,14 May

At art club, we drew one flower from a pot in the middle of the table. I began with a neat circle and added petals around it. ____1____ The real petals overlapped and did not make the regular shape I had expected.

Our tutor asked us to look for one feature before drawing again. I noticed a petal folded partly behind another. ____2____ The second sketch became less tidy but closer to the view in front of me.

My friend was sitting opposite. Her drawing showed a different arrangement. At first I thought one of us must be wrong. ____3____ We were not seeing exactly the same side of the flower.

We put both sketches beside the pot for the final discussion. The tutor did not ask us to select one as the only true picture. ____4____ I kept the first drawing too, because it showed the expectation I had brought to the task.
candidates: A. Each view could preserve something the other did not show.
B. Then we exchanged seats and compared what changed.
C. When I looked up again, the drawing seemed too simple.
D. I began with that particular fold instead of a general circle.
E. Nobody looked at the flower during the session.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C follows idealised first drawing and leads to actual overlap contrast. D revised start/B viewpoint/A combined value belong later; E contradicts observation.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: D names newly observed fold as new starting point, supporting second sketch’s greater fidelity. Others do not describe this redraw.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: B tests opposite positions and prepares different-side explanation. Others address form or final assessment.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A explains keeping multiple views instead of declaring one uniquely true. E denies core activity; other options describe earlier stages.

materials.title: The receipt in the coat pocket
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Saturday,17 May

I found a shop receipt in a coat pocket while helping Dad tidy. It listed a loaf, oranges and a small notebook. I thought it was rubbish and reached for the paper bin. ____1____ He recognised the date before I had read the shop name.

The receipt came from a holiday when we had stayed in a village near the sea. Dad remembered buying the notebook for me after I asked for somewhere to draw the boats. ____2____ The notebook itself was still on my shelf, full of those pictures.

We did not decide to keep every old receipt forever. Dad said this one had a particular connection we wanted to record. ____3____ The note explained why an ordinary list mattered to us, without pretending it was important to everyone.

Later, I looked through the notebook. One boat had a red sail I no longer remembered seeing. The receipt did not prove every detail of the drawing. ____4____ Different records helped us recover different parts of the same day.
candidates: A. Suddenly, the list connected with an object I knew well.
B. The receipt contained a photograph of every boat I drew.
C. Dad asked me to let him look first.
D. But it gave the notebook’s beginning a place and date.
E. We put it in an envelope with a short note.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C interrupts throwing away and introduces Dad recognising date. A notebook link/E kept context/D date-role fit later; B not true of item list.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A connects remembered purchase with extant notebook. Others do not bridge list and familiar object here.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: E preserves selected receipt with context, developed by explanation note. Other options concern discovery/relation rather than storage.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: D limits receipt to origin/place/date, after warning it cannot verify drawn details. B overclaims photos; others earlier actions.

units.title: Two guides: joining a project and giving a comment
units.alignmentNote: Two complete five-gap/seven-candidate guides. Three printed headings, quoted gap2 and heading gap5 retained; two unused options, no extra once-only rule.

materials.title: Joining an ongoing class project
materials.instruction: Read the whole guide. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.
materials.text:
Joining a project after it has started can feel awkward. Other members may use names for files, parts or routines that are unfamiliar to you. ____1____ The aim is to enter the work with enough context, not pretend you already know everything.

Ask a useful first question

A specific question is easier to answer than a general request to explain the whole project. You might say, "____2____" Knowing the immediate task can give the rest of the discussion a clearer place.

Check what has been agreed

Separate decisions already made from ideas still being considered. ____3____ Otherwise, an early suggestion may be repeated as if the group had promised to carry it out.

Take a manageable part

Choose an initial task you can complete and report on. ____4____ A small agreed contribution can teach you more than silently trying to redesign everything at once.

____5____

When the task is finished, tell the group what you did, where the result is and what remains uncertain. This gives others a useful next step and makes it easier for someone else to join later.
candidates: A. What are we trying to finish before the next meeting?
B. Make sure the group understands what you have taken responsibility for.
C. A short summary from one member can make those references easier to follow.
D. Leave a clear handover
E. Starting late means you should never ask any questions.
F. Every suggestion has already become a final decision.
G. Ask where the current decisions are recorded.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C addresses unfamiliar shared references and supplies context. A quoted task question/G decisions/B responsibility/D handover fit later; E/F contradict guide.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A is a concrete question about next deadline/task, fitting quotation and following immediate-task explanation. Other candidates do not ask this question.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: G checks recorded agreed decisions, preventing suggestions being misreported as commitments. Others address entry/task/handover.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: B clarifies the bounded responsibility chosen, developed by small agreed contribution. E/F deny useful participation.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: D is the heading for reporting result/location/uncertainty after completion. Other options do not head a handover paragraph.

materials.title: Giving a useful comment on someone’s work
materials.instruction: Read the whole guide. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.
materials.text:
A comment can help a writer see how a draft is being read. It is less useful when it offers only a verdict with no connection to the words. ____1____ The writer needs something they can examine, not merely a label to accept or reject.

Point to a particular place

Identify the moment that produced your response. You might say, "____2____" That gives the writer a location and an account of what happened during your reading.

Distinguish response from instruction

Saying you were confused is different from requiring one particular rewrite. ____3____ The writer may find another way to address the same difficulty.

Keep the scale reasonable

One reader's reaction does not establish what everyone will feel. ____4____ This makes the comment more accurate without making it less worth hearing.

____5____

After explaining the issue, allow the writer to ask questions or describe the intended effect. You do not need to win an argument. A useful exchange can clarify a choice even when the two people still prefer different versions.
candidates: A. I lost track of who was speaking in the third paragraph.
B. Give a reason or example that supports the judgement.
C. Make room for a reply
D. Every comment must force the writer to use the reader’s exact words.
E. Present the reaction as yours rather than a universal rule.
F. Explain the problem before prescribing your preferred solution.
G. The most helpful feedback never mentions the draft itself.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B develops unsupported verdict into examinable evidence. A quote/F response-solution/E scope/C reply fit later; D/G contradict useful feedback.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A names exact paragraph and reading confusion, matching quote frame and next explanation. Other candidates general advice/headings.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: F distinguishes experienced issue from imposed solution, followed by alternative-rewrite possibility. D incorrectly forces exact wording.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: E limits reaction to observer, matching nonuniversal preceding claim. Others do not address generalisation scope.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C heads the final paragraph about questions and explanation. D/G deny constructive exchange or text connection.
